title: Chapter 66: Saint Clement's, Part 1 of 5: The Letter, Again
html:
Rowan Thorne put on his cadet black in the dark, by feel, the way Master Kross had taught them to dress for a night alarm. Shirt. Stock. Breeches. Boots. Coat. Every button done up from the bottom, so that if you missed one you would know at the top.
He did not miss one.
The room was cold. It was a guest room on the second floor of his aunt's house on the Hill, at the back, over the stable yard, and it had been his room for two years now, but it had never stopped being a guest room. The wallpaper was pale green, with a pattern of small gold baskets of flowers, over and over, hundreds of them, all the same. The bed was too soft. The fire had gone out in the night and nobody had come to light it, because he had told the maid not to. A Thorne did not need a fire to dress for his father's funeral.
Outside, the sky over the roofs was just beginning to go gray. It had snowed again in the night. He could see it on the sill, a thick soft line of it, very white. Below in the yard a groom was sweeping the cobbles, slowly, and the scrape of the broom came up through the glass.
He lit the candle on the washstand and looked at himself in the glass.
The black coat fitted. It had been let out at the shoulders in the autumn and taken in at the waist, and it fitted now the way a cadet's coat ought to fit, close and square. The silver buttons shone. His hair had been cut short the day before, very short, by the cadets' barber in Mercer Street, and it made his ears stand out. He had his father's face. Everyone said so. There was a portrait of his father at twenty that used to hang on the stairs at Crown Walk, and Rowan had stood in front of it many times as a small boy and not seen it, and now he did. The long jaw. The straight brows. The mouth that did not smile easily.
But the eyes were not his father's.
The eyes were his mother's. And his sister's.
He looked away from the glass.
On the washstand, beside the candle, there was a letter.
He had put it there last night, before he went to bed, so that it would be the first thing he saw. It was folded small. Eleven times. He had done that himself, without thinking, the night he got it, and now it would not lie flat anymore. It was creased into a little hard square, the size of a large coin, and the creases had gone soft and furry with handling.
He picked it up.
He knew what it was. He knew it was from Lyra. He knew a girl called Juno had given it to him at the pump in Gallows Lane, at the seventh bell, with snow coming down and her nose running. He could remember the pump, and the snow, and the girl's red nose, and her sharp quick voice saying, "She says read it slow." He could remember taking it, and putting it inside his coat, against his chest, and walking back to the Long Office with his hand pressed flat over it.
He could not remember reading it.
That was the strange thing. That was the thing that kept him awake. He must have read it. He had opened it, he was sure of that, because it had been sealed when Juno gave it to him and now it was not. He had read it, and folded it back up eleven times, and kept it in his breast pocket every day since. But when he tried to think what it said, there was nothing. Not a blank, exactly. More like the place on a wall where a picture has been taken down, and the paper is a different color, and you know a picture was there, and you cannot for the life of you think what it was a picture of.
He did not know how that had happened. He had not burned anything. He was almost sure he had not burned anything. A cadet in his first year was not supposed to burn at all, and he never had, not once, not even a candle's worth. And nobody had taken it out of him. He would have known. Wouldn't he?
He did not know.
So every few days he unfolded it, and read it again.
And every time, it was new.
He unfolded it now. Slowly. Eleven times. The paper was cheap and thin and gray, the kind they sold by the sheet at the stationers on Quill Row, and the writing on it was in pencil. Not Lyra's writing. A big clumsy careful hand, all in capital letters, leaning hard to the right, with some of the letters too big. Somebody had written it for her. He did not know who.
He held it to the candle and read.
And it hit him the way it always did, like cold water. As if he had never seen it before. As if this were the first time.
It said she was alive. It said she was sorry. It said she had not been able to come to him, and that she could not come to him now, and that she was not going to say where she was going, because if she said it, someone might make him tell. It said a thing about their father that made him put his hand flat on the washstand to hold himself up. It said she loved him. It said it twice. And at the bottom, after all the rest, it said one more thing, a short thing, in the same big clumsy capitals.
KEEP COUNTING, RO.
He stood there with the paper in his hand and the candle shaking, and read it through again. And again. Until the words stopped being new and started being words. Until he had it. Until he thought, this time, he would keep it.
He would not. He knew he would not. In three days, or four, he would take it out again, and it would be new again, and it would hit him again like cold water. He did not know why. He only knew it was so.
He folded it back up. Once. Twice. Eleven times. He did not want to. He hated it. He hated that his hands did it on their own, the way Master Kross's hands did it, every day, at his desk in the glass office at the end of the Long Office, folding every scrap of paper that came to him eleven times before he put it away. Rowan had watched him do it for two years. And now his own hands did it too, and he could not make them stop.
He put the hard little square into his breast pocket, inside his coat, on the left side, over his heart. And pressed his hand on it, once.
Then he blew out the candle and went down to breakfast.
Aunt Cressida's Morning Room
The morning room was full of lilies.
It always was. Aunt Cressida had them sent up from the hothouses down by the river at Larkbridge every week, all winter, at a cost Rowan had once worked out on the back of a lesson book and then rubbed out, because it was not a cadet's business. White lilies, tall ones, with long green stems and waxy white trumpets as big as a hand, and orange dust on their tongues that stained the tablecloth if you brushed against them. They stood in tall glass vases on every table and on the mantelpiece and on the windowsills. Today there were more than usual. There were two great vases of them on the breakfast table itself, one at each end, so that you had to lean round them to see across.
And the smell. Heavy and sweet and thick, like warm honey with something under it that was almost rotten. It filled the room. It was in the curtains and the cushions and the walls. It was in Aunt Cressida's hair and her clothes and on her skin, because she wore it too, a scent made from the same lilies, in a small cut-glass bottle on her dressing table. You could smell her coming down a corridor before you saw her. You could smell, in a room, where she had been an hour ago.
Rowan had stopped noticing it, mostly. This morning he noticed it.
The room was on the east side of the house, and the windows looked out over the Hill toward the river, and on a clear morning the sun came in low and gold and lay across the table. This morning there was no sun. The sky over the roofs was a flat white, and the light in the room was gray and cold, and it made the lilies look like wax. The fire was lit. It was the only fire in the house that was always lit, from before dawn until midnight, winter and summer. It roared in the grate and made the room too hot.
Aunt Cressida was already at the table.
She was dressed for the funeral. Black silk, very plain, high at the neck, with long tight sleeves and a row of small jet buttons down the front. A black lace shawl over her shoulders. No pearls. Rowan had never seen her without pearls before, not once in two years, and the bare throat above the black silk looked strange. Too long. Too white.
And her hair.
She wore it as she always did, piled up on top of her head in a high crown of old-gold, smooth and shining, with not one hair out of place. And usually there were the pins. Five silver pins, long ones, each with a small round bead of white glass on the end, pushed into the crown of her hair in a half-circle like the points of a coronet. Ost-glass. They had been her grandmother's. There had been six, once, a wedding gift. She had lost one in the autumn and had not stopped talking about it for a week.
This morning there were no pins.
The crown of hair was there, smooth and high. But it was held with plain black combs, and the white beads were gone.
Rowan looked at the place where they had been. He did not know why it bothered him. Women wore black to funerals. They did not wear white beads in their hair. That was all it was.
"Darling," said Aunt Cressida.
She looked up at him and smiled. It was a bright smile. Too bright. It went across her face very quickly and then stayed there, as if it had been pinned.
"Darling, there you are. Sit down. Sit, sit. You look very fine. Very handsome. Doesn't he look handsome, Pruett?" This to the footman by the sideboard, who bowed and said nothing. "Your father would have been so proud. Sit down and eat something. There's kidneys. There's eggs. There's the smoked fish you like."
Rowan sat. Pruett put a plate in front of him with eggs on it and a piece of fish. He looked at it.
"Eat something, darling," said Aunt Cressida. "People faint at funerals. Especially young men. They stand up straight for too long with their knees locked and down they go, like a tree. I've seen it. At old Lord Ashcombe's, his grandson went down in the middle of the second hymn and knocked over a candle stand. Eat."
He picked up his fork.
She was not eating. She had a cup of chocolate in front of her and a plate with one piece of dry toast on it, and she had not touched either. She was holding the cup in both hands, the way you hold a cup to warm your hands, but the room was too hot for that. Her hands were in black gloves. Thin black kid, buttoned at the wrist.
She was looking at the window.
Not out of it. At it. At the glass. As if she were waiting for something to appear there. A face, or a hand, or a bird.
"Is something wrong, Aunt?" said Rowan.
She turned back to him at once, very quickly, and the bright smile came back.
"Wrong? No. Nothing. What could be wrong? Apart from all of it." She laughed. It was a high, thin, tinkling laugh, like a glass knocked with a spoon. "I was only thinking about the snow. On the steps. They never sweep the steps properly at Saint Clement's. Somebody will slip. I said so to the verger last year and he looked at me as if I'd asked him to sweep the moon." She put down her cup. Picked it up again. "Eat your fish."
He ate some fish. It tasted of nothing.
Aunt Cressida looked at the window.
The lilies smelled. The fire roared. Somewhere in the house a clock struck the half hour, a small silver chime, and Aunt Cressida's cup rattled once against its saucer, very faintly, and was still.
"Rowan," she said.
She said it in a different voice. Lower. Not bright at all. He looked up. She was not smiling now. She was looking at him across the lilies, and there was something in them that he had never seen there before, in two years of breakfasts. He did not know what it was. If she had been anyone else, he would have said it was fear.
"Rowan, darling, after..." She stopped. "After the service. When it's all done. Will you stay with me? Just till the carriage. Don't go off with the other cadets. Don't go off with..." She stopped again. "Just stay with me. Till I'm in the carriage. Will you?"
"Yes, Aunt," said Rowan. "Of course."
"Good." The bright smile came back. It came back so fast that he almost did not see it arrive. "Good. That's settled. Now eat your eggs. You've hardly touched them. Pruett, more chocolate. This has gone cold."
Pruett brought more chocolate.
She did not drink it.
And Rowan sat at the table among the lilies and ate eggs that tasted of nothing and watched his aunt watching the window, and thought about the white beads that were not in her hair, and the bare white throat above the black silk, and the word she had not said. Don't go off with. With whom?
He did not ask.
He had learned, in two years in the Long Office, that the questions people did not let you ask were the only ones worth asking. And that you got the answers to them by keeping quiet, and keeping still, and watching.
The Card on the Tray
The hall of Aunt Cressida's house was tall and cold and white, with a floor of black and white marble squares like a chessboard and a great curving staircase going up one side of it under a dome of colored glass. There were lilies in the hall too. A tall vase of them on the round table in the middle, under the dome, where the light from the colored glass fell on them and turned the white trumpets pink and green and gold.
Beside the vase, on the table, there was a silver tray.
It was where the letters went. Every morning the post came and Pruett put it on the tray, in a neat pile, and Aunt Cressida came down and looked through it with one finger before breakfast, and took what she wanted, and left the rest for her secretary. Cards went there too. Calling cards, left by people who had come to the door and not been let in. On a busy morning in the season there would be twenty of them, white and cream, with names engraved in black, piled up like snow.
This morning there was one.
Rowan saw it as he came down the stairs, with his hand on the cold curved rail. He did not mean to look. He looked because there was only one, and one was strange. On the morning of a funeral, the Hill left cards. It was the thing you did, if you would not come. A card on the tray, to say you were thinking of the family, without having to be seen thinking of it. He had expected a pile.
There was one.
It was cream. Heavy and thick, the kind of card that costs more than a cadet's dinner. And it was not lying flat with the others, because there were no others. It was propped against the vase, standing up on its edge, so that you would see it from the stairs. As if whoever had left it had wanted it seen.
And it was sealed.
Cards were not sealed. Cards had a name on them and nothing else. This one had been folded once, and sealed shut along its edge, with a small round blob of red wax.
Rowan came down the last stairs onto the black and white marble, and crossed to the table, and looked at it. He did not touch it. He was a guest in this house. He did not touch his aunt's post.
But he looked.
On the front of the card, in fine black ink, very neat, there was a name. Not engraved. Written by hand. In a slim, sloping, graceful hand that he did not know.
Lady Cressida Thorne.
And on the seal, pressed into the red wax, there was a mark.
It was very simple. So simple that at first he thought the seal had slipped, and the mark had not taken. It was a circle. Only a circle. A thin, clean, perfect ring, pressed into the wax, with nothing inside it and nothing round it. No crest. No letters. No tree or crown or heron. Just a circle, closed, the size of a fingernail, in red.
He had seen that seal before.
He did not know where. He stood and looked at it and could not think. Somewhere at the Ministry, perhaps. On a paper on Master Kross's desk, that Master Kross had folded eleven times before Rowan could see what was on it. Or on a letter that had come to the Long Office on a Thursday, by a messenger in gray, and been taken straight through to the glass office without being opened. Somewhere. He had seen it, and not thought about it, and now he could not stop thinking about it.
"Rowan, darling. Your coat's not buttoned at the throat."
Aunt Cressida was coming out of the morning room behind him, with Pruett holding her fur cloak.
He turned.
And saw her see the card.
She did not stop walking. She did not change her face. She came across the marble with her small quick steps, saying something about the cold, and how he must keep his throat covered, because the Thornes had weak chests, his grandfather had died of a chest. And as she passed the round table, without looking at it, without pausing, she put out her black-gloved hand and took the card from against the vase, and closed her fingers over it, and went on.
It was done so smoothly that Pruett, behind her with the cloak, did not even turn his head.
By the time she reached the door, the card was gone. Into her glove, or her sleeve, or the little black bag that hung from her wrist. Rowan did not see where. He only saw that her hand was empty, and that she was still talking, about his chest, and about the snow, and about the verger at Saint Clement's who never swept the steps.
And that her voice was a little too high.
Pruett put the fur cloak round her shoulders. She did up the clasp at her throat herself, very quickly, with fingers that fumbled once and then found it.
"Come along, darling," she said. "We'll walk, since you're so set on it. Do up your throat."
Rowan did up his throat.
He did not ask about the card.
But he kept the circle. He took it, the thin red ring in the wax, and put it away carefully, in the place where he kept the things he meant to keep, beside the folded letter and the white beads that were missing from her hair.
